newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER SHOWCASE-TALISMAN HUGHES LOOKING FOR MORE CUP GLORY.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-TALISMAN HUGHES LOOKING FOR MORE CUP GLORY.

text.p: It was late afternoon on a wintry day in west London and Chelsea had just dejectedly trooped off their Stamford Bridge pitch. It was halftime in their F.A. Cup fourth round match against Liverpool and Chelsea, 2-0 down, appeared to be heading out of the Cup.
An hour later they had not only reached the fifth round but had totally demolished Liverpool's self-assurance and defence with four well-taken goals in a 4-2 victory.
The transformation was credited to one man -- 33-year-old Welsh international striker Mark Hughes, who came on as a second half substitute.
Within four minutes of replacing defender Scott Minto he had scored to make it 2-1 and was a talismanic inspiration as Chelsea mounted an epic second-half revival.
It was then that many people had the same thought: "Chelsea's name is on the Cup this season."
Manager Ruud Gullit was full of praise for the Welshman afterwards, who, he said, "had frightened the hell out of the Liverpool defence."

For Hughes it was another chapter in his love affair with the F.A.Cup and on Saturday he could write another even better one. If Chelsea win he will become the first man this century to have played in four F.A. Cup winning teams.
If he scores he would become only the fourth player in history to score for two different teams in the Final -- not including own goals.
George Hedley (Sheffield United 1902, Wolves 1908), Frank Stapleton (Arsenal 1979, Manchester United 1983) and Ian Wright (Crystal Palace 1990, Arsenal 1993) are the only players to have done that.
Hughes previous successes came in 1985, 1990 and 1994 when he scored one of United's goals in their 4-0 win over Chelsea.
He also ended with a losers medal in 1995 when United were beaten by Everton.
He scored twice in United's 3-3 draw with Crystal Palace in 1990 and two more goals on Saturday would bring him level with Ian Rush as the record F.A. Cup final goalscorer.
His career has been an almost continual story of success, but on the eve of the final he revealed that he has only just started to play some of the best football of his long career.
"A lot of my time at United I spent chasing down fullbacks and midfielders, expending a lot of energy doing that instead of attacking."
He said that Gullit stopped him doing that and told him he had just one job in the team. To concentrate on scoring.
"It's taken me 15 years to realise I was playing the game the wrong way."
For much of those 15-years Hughes was in the same Manchester United side as Middlesbrough manager Bryan Robson, team mates when United won the Cup in 1985 and 1990.
Mindful that Middlesbrough have just been relegated and have already lost the League Cup Final this season, Hughes said: "I have great sympathy for Bryan.
"He is a friend of mine and you don't wish that on your worst enemy. But he'll bounce back. He's that sort of man."
Realistic enough at 33 to know there may not be all that many more cup finals ahead, he said he had always loved the big occasion and was certainly determined to enjoy himself on Saturday.
"Certain players love big occasions and enjoy every moment. Others become too tense. I've always liked big occasions.
"The first final I was in when I was 21 or 22 and I enjoyed it even though I didn't play particularly well.

"But I didn't really know what to expect or how to enjoy it properly. I was young, I was a bit on the periphery. Later on I had good friends in the United side and enjoyed it more because I enjoyed it with them."
He's got a very good chance of enjoying it all again on Saturday -- especially if he adds to his personal tally of 26 Cup goals.
"When you start in the game you want to make your mark, and I think I have done that. To win the Cup again would be fantastic."
